article.headline: The EBITDA Multiple Is a Compressed DCF in Disguise
article.lede: The moment a finance student or small-business buyer discovers EBITDA multiples, the appeal is immediate: instead of projecting cash flows across a decade, choosing a discount rate, and sweating over terminal values, one multiplies a single earnings figure by an industry number and arrives at a price. The shortcut is genuine — practitioners use it every day, and major acquisitions are anchored around it. What the discovery tends to skip is how much intellectual work that single multiple is silently performing.
article.body:
*EBITDA* — Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — strips out a company's financing choices and accounting conventions to expose what the business earns from core operations alone. Dividing *enterprise value* (the total claim on the business from all capital holders, including debt) by EBITDA produces the *EV/EBITDA multiple*, a capital-structure-neutral ratio that lets buyers compare a debt-laden manufacturer with an unlevered software firm on the same screen. The ranges, per NYU finance professor Aswath Damodaran's January 2026 sector data, run from roughly 5x for oil-and-gas exploration companies to 35x for semiconductor makers — a spread that encodes vastly different assumptions about growth, competitive durability, and the capital reinvestment required to stay in place.

The underlying insight is mathematically genuine. Under a set of simplifying assumptions — that *depreciation and amortization* roughly equals ongoing capital expenditure, that working capital requirements are stable, that margins and growth hold steady — an EV/EBITDA multiple is algebraically equivalent to a *Gordon Growth Model* DCF. As Damodaran demonstrated formally, the observable market multiple compresses a growth rate, a cost of capital, and a tax rate into one figure. A practitioner using a multiple is not avoiding those assumptions; they are embedding them invisibly in whatever comparable transactions the market has already cleared. When comps are abundant and well-informed, this is an efficient summary of collective analysis. When the peer group is mispriced — as high-growth software was in 2021 — the relative valuation inherits that error without flagging it, where a *discounted cash flow* model would at least force the analyst to name the growth assumption openly.

The most famous objection came from Charlie Munger, who advised substituting the word “bullshit” whenever he heard “EBITDA,” calling it “horror squared.” Warren Buffett’s specific critique is that depreciation is the worst kind of cost — paid in advance, benefited from later — and ignoring it pretends that physical assets do not wear out. For capital-intensive businesses, *D&A* is not an accounting fiction; it is **deferred capital expenditure**. A company reporting $250 million in EBITDA while spending $200 million annually on *maintenance CapEx* — the amount needed merely to preserve existing assets — has vastly different economics from one spending $20 million, yet both look identical on an EV/EBITDA screen. Munger attributed EBITDA’s rise to investment bankers who needed a metric capacious enough to justify the debt loads in *leveraged buyouts*.

The multiple fails most visibly at extremes. For cyclical businesses — commodity producers, airlines, homebuilders — elevated EBITDA at a cycle peak inflates the denominator, making the ratio appear attractively low just when the business is approaching the worst moment to buy it; a trough does the opposite, making cheap assets screen as expensive. High-growth companies often carry minimal or negative EBITDA, rendering the denominator perverse or undefined. Financial institutions cannot be valued this way at all — for a bank, interest income is revenue, not an item to add back. And the *peer-group circularity* problem is always latent: relative valuation assumes the comparable companies are correctly priced. When an entire sector is exuberant, every name within it will screen as fairly valued against its neighbors, with the shared mispricing invisible from inside the method.

In practice, professional buyers use multiples and discounted cash flow analysis as complements, not substitutes. A multiple anchors the opening bid and makes price discovery fast in a competitive auction. A DCF tests whether the implied assumptions behind that multiple — the growth rate, the reinvestment rate, the cost of capital — are defensible given the specific business. *Precedent transactions* — actual deals cleared in the same sector — reveal what acquirers paid under real competitive pressure, including the control premium that a public-market comparison will understate. When all three methods converge on a similar number, the valuation is defensible. When they diverge, the divergence is diagnostic. The discovery the post describes is real: EBITDA multiples can price a stable, mature, asset-light business quickly and credibly. Applying a multiple without asking what growth rate and capital requirement it silently implies is not escaping the work of a DCF — it is hiding that work from oneself.

concepts.definition: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization. A measure of a company's operating performance that strips out financing choices, tax jurisdiction, and non-cash accounting entries, allowing comparison across companies with very different capital structures or depreciation policies.

Enterprise Value divided by EBITDA. The dominant valuation ratio in M&A and investment analysis because it is capital-structure-neutral — it compares the total cost to acquire a business (including its debt) against its operating earnings, enabling comparison between leveraged and unleveraged firms.

The total cost of acquiring a company, accounting for all financial claimants. Calculated as market capitalization plus net debt (total debt minus cash), plus preferred equity and minority interests. It represents what a buyer would need to pay to own the business free and clear of all obligations.

A simplified discounted cash flow formula that assumes cash flows grow at a constant rate in perpetuity, producing a single-equation value: current cash flow divided by (discount rate minus growth rate). It is mathematically equivalent to EV/EBITDA under idealized assumptions about capital expenditure, working capital, and growth stability.

Non-cash accounting charges that spread the cost of long-lived assets — factories, equipment, acquired intangibles — over their useful lives. EBITDA adds D&A back on the premise that they are not real cash outlays; critics note this is only true to the extent assets do not need to be replaced, which is rarely the case in capital-intensive industries.

The capital expenditure required to preserve a business's existing productive capacity, as distinct from growth CapEx invested in expansion. High maintenance CapEx means real cash is leaving the business to replace worn assets — a cost EBITDA ignores entirely, making EV/EBITDA multiples potentially misleading for asset-heavy companies.

An acquisition financed largely with borrowed money, using the acquired company's own assets and future cash flows as collateral. LBO analysis leans heavily on EBITDA because the ratio of acquisition debt to EBITDA determines how much leverage a deal can sustain before debt service overwhelms cash generation.

The logical problem inherent in relative valuation: a multiple derived from comparable companies assumes those companies are correctly priced by the market. If an entire sector is overvalued, every firm within it will screen as fairly priced against its neighbors, embedding the shared mispricing invisibly into the valuation.

A valuation method that projects a company's future free cash flows over an explicit forecast period, then discounts them back to the present using a risk-adjusted rate. Unlike multiples, it forces the analyst to state growth, margin, and discount-rate assumptions explicitly — a theoretical strength that is also its primary vulnerability to manipulation.

Historical M&A deals in the same sector, used as valuation benchmarks. They reveal what real acquirers paid under competitive auction conditions, typically including a control premium above public-market prices. Alongside trading multiples and DCF, they form the third leg of the standard valuation triangle.

article.fact_check: The tweet makes no explicit factual claim — it is a humorous observation about discovering a simpler valuation approach. The implicit suggestion that an EBITDA multiple is a straightforward substitute for a DCF is valid for stable, mature, asset-light businesses but misleading as a general principle: the shortcut does not eliminate assumptions about growth, capital reinvestment, and risk — it encodes them invisibly in the market multiple. For capital-intensive, cyclical, financial, or high-growth businesses, the substitution can produce seriously incorrect valuations.
